name: separated-domain-model
intent: Keep an explicit, behaviour-bearing domain model deliberately distinct from the data model, translating between the two in an explicit mapper/repository layer so that neither the storage shape constrains the model nor model changes reshape the schema.
problem: The domain model and the data model keep collapsing into each other: ORMs, schemas and transport formats push annotations, base classes, proxies or table-shaped fields into the classes that hold business rules, so a column rename becomes a domain change and the model can no longer be reasoned about, tested or refactored on its own. The reverse failure is just as common - an explicit domain model is rejected as too much work because nobody owns the translation between model and storage.
context: Applies where the domain has behaviour and invariants worth protecting and the storage shape (relational schema, document format, legacy database, ORM conventions) would otherwise dictate the model: DDD and hexagonal codebases, systems with several representations of the same data (database, API, events), migrations between stores, and teams that want to test domain rules without a database. It is a deliberate decision rather than a framework default - the model stays explicit only if the mapper is an owned, tested part of the codebase.
benefits: Business rules are expressed in domain terms: invariants, value objects and the ubiquitous language are not bent to fit tables, columns or framework conventions.
The model is testable in memory - no database, no ORM session, no fixtures - so domain tests run in milliseconds and stay deterministic.
Storage can change without touching the model: swapping the ORM, splitting the schema, moving to a document store or adding a read database edits the mapping layer only.
Persistence mechanics (identity maps, dirty tracking, lazy loading, proxies, optimistic locking) stay behind the boundary instead of leaking into business rules and callers.
Write model and read model can diverge on purpose: aggregates enforce invariants while projections answer queries in the shape their consumers need.
The mapper is a single, explicit place where the shape differences between model and storage are handled - useful for legacy schemas, multi-table value objects and versioned documents.
tradeoffs: Two models plus the code between them: every new field needs mapping on both sides, and the mapping is bookkeeping nobody gets credit for.
The ORM's conveniences are lost for the separated model: change tracking, identity and cascading saves have to be re-created with a Unit of Work or explicit repository saves.
Mapping becomes a new failure surface - silently dropped, renamed or mis-ordered fields, invalid rehydration, and N+1 queries when relations are loaded implicitly.
Extra objects and copies per read and write; heavy aggregate graphs must be loaded deliberately, which costs both code and latency.
It only pays off with discipline: without ownership the separated model degenerates into an anemic duplicate of the tables and every change is made twice.
Tooling friction: generated clients, migration tools and IDE navigation assume the persistent type is the model, so the team has to maintain conventions for the mapping layer.

participants.responsibility: Explicit types named after domain concepts - entities, value objects, aggregates - that own behaviour and invariants and carry no persistence, transport or framework concerns.
The storage-shaped representation: rows, documents, DAOs or ORM entities whose fields match the schema, kept in the infrastructure layer and never handed to callers.
Translates between the two models in both directions, field by field and without business logic; it is the only component that knows both shapes.
Owns access to storage: it queries, hydrates the domain model through validating constructors and saves it again, speaking only in domain types to its callers.
Tracks the objects a use case touched and flushes them in one transaction, restoring the change-tracking the domain model deliberately does not carry itself.

use_cases: A rich domain model (money, policies, multi-step invariants) whose data sits in a legacy or awkward schema that cannot be reshaped - the mapper acts as an anti-corruption layer.
The same domain served by more than one store, or migrated between stores, so the model must survive a change of persistence technology untouched.
A bounded context whose model must diverge from an upstream database it does not control, while the database keeps its own shape.
Systems where the domain must be unit-tested without a database: pricing, eligibility and lifecycle rules verified in memory, with mapping covered by separate round-trip tests.
Read-heavy applications where write aggregates enforce invariants while query objects or projections feed the UI in a different shape.
Regulated domains where explicit mapping documents which fields enter and leave the model, and internal state must never be exposed accidentally.

Python services built around plain dataclasses keep SQLAlchemy out of the domain class entirely: the ORM mapping is attached from the infrastructure side with registry.mapped() or map_imperatively(), so the model never carries ORM instrumentation even though SQLAlchemy still does the persistence.

Microsoft's .NET microservice guidance organizes each service as a Domain.Model project of persistence-ignorant POCO aggregates plus an infrastructure layer owning the Entity Framework DbContext and repositories, so business code references no persistence package at all.

Java services built on jOOQ keep generated Record types inside the query layer and translate results into hand-written domain POJOs through a RecordMapper or constructor-based mapping, so jOOQ types never appear in business code.
avoid_when: The application is CRUD over a data model that already expresses the rules: Active Record or a table/row gateway is simpler and honest.
The domain has no invariants beyond field validation, so the second model would only duplicate the first - keep the data model and validate at the boundary.
The chosen ORM can map the domain types as they are (fluent configuration, externalized metadata, typeclass instances): use that instead of adding a second model and a DAO layer.
Reads dominate and no behaviour runs on the result: query the database into DTOs/projections rather than round-tripping through aggregates.
The team has no owner for the mapping layer and no tests around it; a separated model without that discipline costs more than it returns.
anti_patterns: An anemic domain model that mirrors the table field for field: two models, double bookkeeping and no behaviour protected - the mapping code buys nothing.
Persistence annotations, ORM base classes or table-shaped fields on the domain types, with the separation claimed only in documentation.
Repository interfaces that return ORM entities, query-builder handles or lazy proxies, so every caller keeps speaking the database dialect.
Convention- or reflection-based mapping without round-trip tests: fields are silently dropped, renamed or reordered and invalid states enter the model on load.
Rebuilding objects by bypassing constructors - field assignment, JSON deserialization or framework rehydration hooks - so value-object validation and invariants never run.
Routing every read through the write model: report and list screens round-tripping rows through aggregates instead of using a read model or query object.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: the domain model depends on nothing in the infrastructure; the ORM, schema and driver depend on the model, not the other way round.
Separation of concerns: business rules, storage shape and translation are three responsibilities with three different owners.
Persistence ignorance: the model does not know a database exists - it exposes domain operations, not columns, tables or SQL.
Single responsibility for translation: mapping is its own module with no business logic, and no business logic hides in mappers.
Encapsulation: values enter the model only through constructors, factories or domain operations that can reject them.
Explicit over implicit at the boundary: prefer visible field-by-field mapping to conventions or reflection that hide what is translated.
best_practices: Keep domain types free of persistence, transport and framework concerns; if a mapping annotation or base class is needed, put it on the data model instead.
Write one mapper per aggregate with explicit field assignment, keep it free of business logic, and cover it with round-trip tests against realistic row shapes.
Hydrate through validating constructors or factories; never rebuild domain objects by property assignment or convention-based copying.
Let repositories speak only in domain types and collections - never hand back rows, ORM entities, query builders or proxies.
Add a separate persistence model only where the storage genuinely diverges; otherwise configure the ORM to map the domain types directly.
Own the transaction boundary explicitly with a Unit of Work or repository-scoped transaction, since domain objects no longer carry their own persistence lifecycle.
Version the mapping together with the schema: a migration is a mapping change, not just a table change.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) - Domain Model (Domain Logic Patterns) and Data Mapper (Object-Relational Structural Patterns).
Evans, Domain-Driven Design (2003) - Model-Driven Design, layered architecture and persistence ignorance; Vernon, Implementing Domain-Driven Design (2013) - aggregates and repositories.
Khorikov, 'When do you need a persistence model?' (2020) - the counter-argument that the database schema plus the ORM already is a persistence model.
Microsoft patterns & practices, Project Silk - server-side guidance on deciding whether to create a separate domain model that is distinct from the data model.
Percival & Gregory, Architecture Patterns with Python (2020) - repository chapter: inverting the ORM/domain dependency with SQLAlchemy imperative ('classical') mapping.
